record.title: A preprint reports that live tool-progress signals improved post-tool latency in one serving-engine experiment
record.summary: Liu et al. propose exposing execution progress from running agent tools to the serving system for KV-cache decisions. Their preprint reports a harness reading progress from tool output and environment state without changing the agent-visible result path, and an end-to-end experiment in a production engine. The authors report 20.7% lower p90 time to first token after tool calls with HBM only and 20.8% with HBM plus DRAM compared with LRU. These are paper-reported results, not an independent reproduction or evidence of general serving-system gains.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: Liu, Zhang, Li and Zhang posted arXiv:2609.18849v1 on 2026-09-16, proposing that agent tools expose live progress to guide serving-side KV-cache decisions.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that their harness recovered progress signals from four public agent corpora and that the signals improved prediction accuracy at tested KV-cache decision points.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the authors’ end-to-end production-engine experiment, live progress-based scheduling reduced p90 time to first token after a tool call by 20.7% in an HBM-only configuration and 20.8% with HBM plus DRAM versus LRU.

evidence_gaps.description: The p90 post-tool TTFT improvements are author-reported; the research desk did not run the experiment or audit full workload/hardware details.

brief.importance_rationale: If the measured improvement holds, live progress reporting could materially improve KV-cache scheduling and responsiveness for tool-heavy agent serving, a useful but bounded systems result; one paper’s evaluation does not establish broad deployment impact.
limitations: Results are from one author-reported preprint evaluation; no independent replication or peer review was established in this check.
A bounded search did not locate an inspectable author implementation or independent rerun; this is not proof none exists.
The 20.7% and 20.8% figures are p90 time-to-first-token after tool calls in two reported memory configurations; they are not general end-to-end agent latency or throughput gains.
Some tool calls expose no parseable progress, and the method depends on signals available from the tool or harness.

Their preprint reports a harness reading progress from tool output and environment state without changing the agent-visible result path, and an end-to-end experiment in a production engine. The authors report 20.7% lower p90 time to first token after tool calls with HBM only and 20.8% with HBM plus DRAM compared with LRU. These are paper-reported results, not an independent reproduction or evidence of general serving-system gains.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report 20.7% and 20.8% lower p90 post-tool TTFT versus LRU in HBM-only and HBM+DRAM configurations.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint describes the proposed method and reported evaluation; the research desk did not reproduce it.
technical.mechanism: A harness surfaces tool progress from output/execution state through a separate event path; a serving controller uses estimated remaining time for KV-cache retention, eviction and prefetch.
technical.regime: One author-reported production-engine evaluation; workload mix and hardware need fuller audit; no broad serving-stack transfer established.
technical.strongest_baseline: LRU for end-to-end p90 post-tool TTFT; four published predictors for prediction accuracy.

brief.title: A preprint reports that live tool-progress signals improved post-tool latency in one serving-engine experiment
brief.why_it_matters: Tool execution can leave an agent request’s KV cache occupying scarce GPU memory while the agent waits. If the reported gains transfer, live tool progress could improve post-tool responsiveness and cache scheduling. Current evidence supports a specific paper-reported result, not a general performance guarantee.
